word:hebrew:H1016.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to Beth Dagon, a place name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in the book of Joshua: twice in Joshua 15:41 and twice in Joshua 19:27. The English rendering preserves the name as “Beth” and “Dagon.” Without verse text, the name itself identifies the location, while the surrounding passage determines its role in each boundary or city-list setting.

word:hebrew:H1139.explanation: This Hebrew word functions as a proper name, rendered “Bene.” It identifies a named location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both within Joshua 19:45, so its use is limited and highly specific. The available lexical information does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond this name. Its precise significance in Joshua 19:45 depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:hebrew:H1175.explanation: Bealoth is a Hebrew place-name, identifying a location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, once in Joshua 15:24 and once in 1 Kings 4:16. The available biblical renderings preserve it as “Bealoth,” so its ordinary meaning is the name of a place. The exact significance of that location in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:hebrew:H125.explanation: This Hebrew word describes something that is reddish in color. It functions as a color term, identifying a visible red or red-tinged appearance rather than naming an object or action. It occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Leviticus, where it helps describe visible conditions examined under Israel’s laws. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the thing being described, but its basic sense remains a reddish appearance.

word:hebrew:H1254.explanation: Bara means to create, as when God created the heavens and the earth. It can also describe cutting down a forest.

word:hebrew:H1298.explanation: Bera is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word appears only once, and its English rendering is consistently “Bera.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes one person from others in the biblical record. The surrounding verse provides the specific historical setting, but the word itself serves as a personal designation.

word:hebrew:H1320.explanation: Basar means flesh. It can also refer to the body as a whole, and it can name flesh eaten as food.

word:hebrew:H1386.explanation: Gabnon means a hump or peak of hills. It can also describe hills as high.

word:hebrew:H1412.explanation: Gudgodah is a Hebrew place-name, rendered “Gudgodah.” It refers to a named location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Deuteronomy 10:7. The available information identifies the name and its use as a location, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the place’s geography or significance. Its precise role in that verse therefore depends on the surrounding context.

word:hebrew:H1467.explanation: This Hebrew word means “pride,” referring to an elevated view of oneself or one’s status. It functions as a noun naming this attitude or condition. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 4:37, so its ordinary scriptural use is represented by that single occurrence. The surrounding verse provides the specific setting, while the word itself identifies pride as the subject being named.

word:hebrew:H1603.explanation: Gaal is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H169.explanation: Ohel is a personal name, referring to a particular individual rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears only once, at 1 Chronicles 3:20, and English translations preserve it as “Ohel.” Because it is a name, its basic meaning is the person it identifies; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s place or significance in the passage.

word:hebrew:H1746.explanation: Dumah is the name of a tribe. It is also used as a place name.

word:hebrew:H1874.explanation: Darkon is a Hebrew personal name, preserved in English as “Darkon.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus: once in Ezra 2:56 and once in Nehemiah 7:58. Because no short definition or descriptive meaning is provided, its supported sense is the name itself, with the surrounding passage needed to clarify the person or family identified there.

word:hebrew:H1940.explanation: Hodiah is a personal name for a Jewess.

word:hebrew:H2000.explanation: Hâmam means to put into confusion or commotion. It can mean to disturb. It can also mean to destroy.

word:hebrew:H2181.explanation: Zanah describes sexual immorality, including acting as a prostitute. It can also describe idolatry, when people forsake Yahweh and pursue other gods.

word:hebrew:H2211.explanation: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra 6:11. No direct English gloss or short definition is available here, so its precise meaning cannot be stated more narrowly without adding information that is not provided. The word functions within that single verse, and the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its force there accurately.

word:hebrew:H2332.explanation: Chavvah means Eve, the first woman.

word:hebrew:H2347.explanation: Chus means to pity or show compassion. It can also mean to spare someone.

word:hebrew:H240.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a “weapon,” an object used for fighting. It functions as a noun, naming an implement rather than an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Deuteronomy 23:13, so its normal lexical sense is narrowly attested in this corpus. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how the weapon is being discussed there; the word itself identifies the implement.

word:hebrew:H2541.explanation: Chamots means violent. It can also mean oppressed.

word:hebrew:H2615.explanation: In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word refers to “Hannathon,” a named designation preserved in English rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs once, in Joshua 19:14, so its normal use is limited to that single occurrence. No broader lexical sense is established here; the word’s role is to identify Hannathon within the biblical text. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H2659.explanation: Châphêr means to be ashamed or confounded. It can also mean to put someone to shame.

word:hebrew:H2736.explanation: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Harhaiah.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Nehemiah 3:8. Because no lexical definition or explanatory verse text is available here, its underlying name meaning cannot be stated reliably. Its role is therefore best understood as identifying the person named Harhaiah in that passage.

word:hebrew:H2790.explanation: Chârash means to be silent or hold one's peace.

word:hebrew:H2835.explanation: Chasiph means a small company drawn off or separated from the rest, as with two little flocks.

word:hebrew:H2879.explanation: This Hebrew word is a rare term whose ordinary meaning cannot be stated confidently from the available lexical information. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 8:13, but no explicit definition or English rendering is available here. The reference identifies where it occurs, not what the word means by itself. Its precise sense therefore requires the verse text and surrounding context.

word:hebrew:H2897.explanation: Tob is the name of a region, apparently east of the Jordan.

word:hebrew:H3018.explanation: Yegia means toil or labor—the work a person does.

word:hebrew:H3043.explanation: Jediael is a personal name used for individuals in the Old Testament. It identifies people recorded in genealogical and military lists, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in 1 Chronicles, including passages about family lines, warriors, and gatekeepers. Its precise significance as a name is not defined here, but its repeated use consistently functions as a person's identifying name.

word:hebrew:H3106.explanation: Jubal is a personal name, identifying a particular man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 4:21, and is rendered “Jubal.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning here is primarily identifying: it points to the person called Jubal. The surrounding verse gives the context for his role, while the word itself serves as his name.

word:hebrew:H3227.explanation: Yeminiy means right. It can also describe something on the right hand.

word:hebrew:H3252.explanation: Iscah is a personal name, rendered as “Iscah.” It identifies one individual rather than describing an action, object, or quality. This Hebrew word occurs once, in Genesis 11:29, so its ordinary meaning is limited to this name rather than a broader vocabulary concept. The name itself does not provide a general definition or a wider category of meaning; the surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

word:hebrew:H3285.explanation: Jaanai is a Hebrew personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, in 1 Chronicles 5:12. Since it functions as a name, its significance here is the person it identifies, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about that person. The name is rendered “Jaanai” in the cited translation.

word:hebrew:H3331.explanation: Yatsa means to spread something over a surface. It can also mean to make a bed.

word:hebrew:H3450.explanation: This Hebrew word is a personal name appearing once in the Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:36. The available information identifies the Hebrew name but does not provide a gloss, definition, translation, or verse text that explains what the name itself means. Therefore, its safest plain-language sense is simply the name of a person, while any deeper meaning would require additional scriptural or lexical evidence. Its occurrence is limited to this single reference.

word:hebrew:H3502.explanation: Yithrah refers to wealth—abundance or riches.

word:hebrew:H3577.explanation: Kazab means falsehood or untruth. It is also used for lies and deceitful things.

word:hebrew:H3599.explanation: Kis means a cup; it can also mean a bag or purse for money or weights.

word:hebrew:H3609.explanation: Chileab is a personal name, referring to one individual in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is not presented with an explicit definition or descriptive gloss, so its ordinary lexical meaning cannot be stated beyond recognizing it as a name. The name occurs once, in 2 Samuel 3:3. English renderings preserve it as “Chileab,” rather than translating it into a descriptive phrase. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

word:hebrew:H3645.explanation: Kemosh is the name of the god of the Moabites.

word:hebrew:H3692.explanation: Chislon is a Hebrew proper name, rendered “Chislon,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 34:21. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain the person’s role. Its precise significance in that verse therefore depends on the surrounding biblical passage, not on an added meaning for the name itself.

word:hebrew:H37.explanation: Abital is a personal name, functioning as the identifying name of an individual rather than as a common word with a stated descriptive meaning. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, and both English renderings preserve it as “Abital.” Because no short definition or gloss is provided, its significance here is its role as a proper name; the surrounding verse is needed for any passage-specific explanation.

word:hebrew:H374.explanation: Ephah means a measure, especially a measure for grain. It can also be used more generally for a measure.

word:hebrew:H3744.explanation: This Hebrew word means “herald,” referring to a person who publicly announces a message or command. It functions as a noun and appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 3:4. Its limited occurrence means the word’s broader range cannot be established from repeated biblical usage, but its basic sense is clear: an official announcer who communicates something publicly on behalf of another. The surrounding verse provides the specific setting for its use.

word:hebrew:H3788.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to an “advantage,” identifying what is favorable or useful in a situation. It functions as the thing being considered when a passage speaks about what someone gains, possesses, or finds worthwhile. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament, all in Ecclesiastes, showing a focused use rather than a broadly distributed term. Its occurrences can also appear in contexts involving what is given or received.

word:hebrew:H3807.explanation: Kathath means to bruise. It can also describe beating people down.

word:hebrew:H3872.explanation: Luchith is a place east of the Jordan.

word:hebrew:H3951.explanation: Leqet means gleaning, the portion of a harvest left ungathered in the field rather than collected with the rest.

word:hebrew:H4002.explanation: Mabbûwaʻ means a fountain or spring.

word:hebrew:H4077.explanation: This Hebrew word means “Median,” serving as a name or identifying term for someone or something associated with the Median people. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Daniel 5:31. Because the available information gives the word’s identifying sense but not the verse text, its precise role in that sentence must be understood from Daniel 5:31 and its surrounding passage. The word itself functions chiefly to identify Median origin or association.

word:hebrew:H4099.explanation: Medatha is the name of Haman’s father.

word:hebrew:H4150.explanation: Mo'ed means an appointed time or season. It can also refer to a gathering or meeting place, as with the Tent of Meeting.

word:hebrew:H42.explanation: Abinoam is the personal name of an Israelite; Scripture identifies him as Barak’s father.

word:hebrew:H424.explanation: Elah means an oak or another strong tree.

word:hebrew:H4244.explanation: Mahlah is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a woman rather than describing an action, object, or quality. It is rendered “Mahlah” in the English references and occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament. The name appears in several passages concerning the same named person and is also connected with a genealogical birth record. Its meaning here is therefore chiefly identifying: it marks Mahlah as an individual within Israel’s recorded family history.

word:hebrew:H4345.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a grate or grating: a structured surface made with openings. It is used six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Exodus, for a component of the tabernacle’s furnishings. As a noun, it names the physical object itself rather than an action or quality. The repeated use in descriptions of the altar shows that the word belongs to the practical vocabulary of constructing and arranging sacred equipment.

word:hebrew:H4406.explanation: Millah means a word. It can also refer to a matter or thing. It can also denote a command.

word:hebrew:H4518.explanation: Menaqqith means a sacrificial basin for holding blood.

word:hebrew:H4543.explanation: Miskenah means a magazine or storehouse, a place for storing goods. It can also mean treasure, as in treasure cities.

word:hebrew:H4631.explanation: This Hebrew noun means “cave,” referring to a natural hollow or underground place. It is used across the Old Testament for a physical location, and its 38 occurrences show that this is an established everyday noun rather than a rare or specialized expression. The word appears in passages from Genesis through Ezekiel, including references associated with burial places, hiding places, and other locations described as caves.

word:hebrew:H4727.explanation: This Hebrew word means “taking,” describing the act of taking something. It functions as an action term rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 19:7. Because it appears only once and no broader definition is provided, “taking” is the clearest supported sense. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

word:hebrew:H4752.explanation: Mar means a drop, as in a drop in a bucket.

word:hebrew:H4785.explanation: Marah is the name of a place in the desert.

word:hebrew:H4929.explanation: Mishmar means a guard, a place of custody, or a watch.

word:hebrew:H4965.explanation: This Hebrew expression refers to a specific term whose precise English meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 2 Samuel 8:1. The wording functions as an expression rather than a clearly defined everyday action or quality. Its exact sense must therefore remain tied to the wording and broader context of that verse, rather than being expanded into an unsupported translation or interpretation.

word:hebrew:H5056.explanation: This Hebrew word means “push,” describing forceful thrusting against something. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Exodus 21, where the surrounding law discusses an animal’s repeated or dangerous behavior. Its basic sense is therefore an active, forceful shove or thrust, rather than a general movement. The exact force intended in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but “push” is the supported meaning for this word.

word:hebrew:H5171.explanation: Nachăray is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H521.explanation: Ammah means cubit, a measure used for height or width.

word:hebrew:H5214.explanation: Nîyr means to till the soil. It can also describe breaking up fallow ground.

word:hebrew:H5283.explanation: Naaman is a personal name. It names a son of Benjamin and a captain of the king of Syria.

word:hebrew:H5360.explanation: Neqamah means vengeance—the act of avenging.

word:hebrew:H5430.explanation: This Hebrew word means “battle” and functions as a term naming such an event. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Isaiah 9:5. The available rendering consistently gives “battle,” supporting this central sense. Because the word appears only once and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the larger context of Isaiah 9:5 rather than from the word alone.

word:hebrew:H5496.explanation: Sooth means to stimulate someone. It can also mean to persuade or entice someone.

word:hebrew:H5522.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a “tabernacle,” functioning as a noun that names a thing. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Amos 5:26. Because it appears only once and no verse text is available here, its broader use cannot be established from this word record alone. Its basic sense is therefore the named object, “tabernacle,” while the surrounding passage supplies the specific force of the reference.

word:hebrew:H5557.explanation: Salaph means to subvert or pervert.

word:hebrew:H5728.explanation: This word means “yet.” It marks something that continues or remains the case, often carrying the thought forward despite what has just been said. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ecclesiastes 4:2–3. Its precise force in each sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its normal function is to express continuing comparison or a further point in the argument. (Ecclesiastes 4:2; 4:3)

word:hebrew:H5773.explanation: This Hebrew word means “perverse.” It functions as a descriptive term, presenting something as perverse rather than naming a person, place, or action by itself. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 19:14. That single occurrence identifies its basic sense, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes there. The word’s normal force is therefore concise: it marks something as perverse within the sentence where it occurs.

word:hebrew:H5801.explanation: Izzavon means trade. It can refer to the wares exchanged or to the fair where trading takes place.

word:hebrew:H5953.explanation: ʻAlal means to do or work something thoroughly. It can also describe gleaning a vineyard after gathering its grapes, mocking someone, or abusing someone.

word:hebrew:H6040.explanation: Onî means misery, affliction, or trouble.

word:hebrew:H617.explanation: Assir is a personal name used for two Israelites.

word:hebrew:H6174.explanation: ʻÂrôwm means naked or nude, whether partly or completely unclothed.

word:hebrew:H6325.explanation: Punon is a place-name, rendered as “Punon,” rather than an ordinary descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 33:42–43. The available material identifies it as a named location, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the location’s identity or significance. Its meaning is therefore the place-name “Punon,” with its specific reference understood from the surrounding biblical context.

word:hebrew:H6369.explanation: Pîykôl is a personal name, rendered Phichol in English. Its bearer is identified as the chief captain of an army.

word:hebrew:H6387.explanation: This Hebrew word describes dividing—separating something into parts or portions. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 7:25, so its normal lexical meaning is supported by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of passages. In that sentence, it functions as an action or process involving division. The precise force of the word in Daniel 7:25 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

word:hebrew:H6417.explanation: This Hebrew word means “judgment.” It names a judicial decision or ruling rather than describing a person, place, or action in general. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 28:7, so its normal meaning is supported by that single scriptural occurrence. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the word functions there, but the central idea remains judgment: a formal assessment or decision concerning what is right or wrong.

word:hebrew:H6462.explanation: Pispah is a personal name, rendered “Pispah” in English. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. This Hebrew name appears only once in the Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:38. Because no explicit lexical definition or surrounding verse text is available here, the name itself should not be assigned an additional meaning beyond identifying the person named Pispah.

word:hebrew:H6523.explanation: Parzel means iron. In Scripture, iron is used as a comparison for strength because it breaks in pieces and crushes.

word:hebrew:H6578.explanation: Perath is the name of the Euphrates, a river.

word:hebrew:H662.explanation: Afak means to restrain or control oneself.

word:hebrew:H6624.explanation: Pathros is the name of a part of Egypt.

word:hebrew:H6721.explanation: Tsidon is the name of Canaan’s son. It also names a place.

word:hebrew:H6839.explanation: This Hebrew word means “Zophim,” functioning as a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive term. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 23:14, and the English rendering preserves it as “Zophim.” Because no verse text or explicit definition is available here, the safest understanding is simply the name itself; its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding biblical context.

word:hebrew:H6875.explanation: Tsᵉrîy means balm, a medicinal substance.

word:hebrew:H6916.explanation: Qiddah means cassia bark, called cassia in English. Scripture lists it with oil and also names it among merchandise.

word:hebrew:H7029.explanation: Kishi is a personal name, rendered “Kishi” in English. It identifies an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 6:44, and the available wording preserves it as a name without giving a separate descriptive definition. Its precise significance as a personal name is therefore not established here; readers should understand it primarily as the identifying name of a person in that genealogy.

word:hebrew:H7065.explanation: Qana means to be zealous. It can also describe being jealous or envious.

word:hebrew:H7191.explanation: Kishion is a proper place-name, referring to a location named in the Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Bible’s recorded Old Testament occurrences, both in Joshua: Joshua 19:20 and Joshua 21:28. Since no verse text is included here, the name’s precise role in each passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense is the location called Kishion.

word:hebrew:H723.explanation: Urva means a herding-place for an animal, such as a stall.

word:hebrew:H7234.explanation: Rabad means to spread or deck out.

word:hebrew:H7326.explanation: Ruwsh means to be destitute or poor.

word:hebrew:H7380.explanation: Ribai is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea or action. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, with the same English rendering, “Ribai,” in both occurrences. The name is found in 2 Samuel 23:29 and 1 Chronicles 11:31. Those references identify its limited, name-like use, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in either passage.

word:hebrew:H7407.explanation: Rokes means pride in this usage.

word:hebrew:H7472.explanation: Rei is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 1:8, and is rendered as “Rei.” Because it functions as a person’s name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who is being mentioned. The surrounding verse is needed to explain Rei’s role in that passage, but the word itself is the name of this individual.

word:hebrew:H7551.explanation: Raqam means to embroider or make needlework in varied colors.

word:hebrew:H7713.explanation: Sederah means a row or rank; it can also mean boards in a house.

word:hebrew:H7748.explanation: This Hebrew word is a proper name rendered “Shuham.” It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader meaning, but as a name used once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Numbers 26:42. The available rendering consistently gives “Shuham,” so that name is the clearest way to understand it. Its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context, which is not included here.

word:hebrew:H7784.explanation: Shûwq means a street or streets.

word:hebrew:H7850.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a “scourge,” functioning as a noun for something that brings severe affliction or punishment. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 23:13. The word’s basic sense is therefore an instrument or means of painful trouble, while the surrounding verse determines its precise force in that passage. Its recorded use is connected with something given or appointed, helping show that the word describes a scourge as an object rather than an action.

word:hebrew:H7902.explanation: Shekabah means a lying down, including dew lying on the ground. It can also refer to the sexual act.

word:hebrew:H7977.explanation: Shilchi is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H7999.explanation: Shalam means to complete or carry out something. It can also mean paying what is owed or making restitution. In another use, it describes being at peace.

word:hebrew:H8015.explanation: Shelomi is the personal name “Shelomi,” referring to an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word or action, but as a person’s name. The name occurs once in the Hebrew corpus, at Numbers 34:27. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific role in that passage cannot be explained further; its supported lexical function is simply identification by name.

word:hebrew:H8059.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a “release,” especially the letting go of what is owed. In Deuteronomy, it names the appointed release associated with debts and with a recurring period established for Israel. The word appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Deuteronomy, where it functions as something Israel was to observe and proclaim. Its surrounding context determines the precise application in each verse, but its central idea is release rather than continued demand or retention.

word:hebrew:H8136.explanation: Shin’an means repetition, as in repeated or multiplied numbers.

word:hebrew:H8190.explanation: Shaashgaz is a Hebrew personal name, not a common word describing an idea, action, or quality. It refers to a particular person in the Old Testament and appears only once, in Esther 2:14. Since no explicit definition is preserved, its ordinary meaning cannot be expanded beyond the name itself. English Bibles render it “Shaashgaz,” so readers should treat it as a person’s name rather than translate it as a descriptive term.

word:hebrew:H8204.explanation: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Shiphtan.” It identifies one individual in the Hebrew Old Testament and does not function as a general description, action, or quality. The name occurs once, in Numbers 34:24. Because no broader definition or additional occurrences are available here, its ordinary meaning is best stated as the person’s name rather than expanded into an unsupported symbolic or conceptual meaning.

word:hebrew:H8293.explanation: Shêrûwth means freedom, though one passage renders it as remnant.

word:hebrew:H8341.explanation: Shâshâh means to divide into sixths or to give a sixth part.

word:hebrew:H8547.explanation: Tamah is a Hebrew personal name. It appears twice in the Old Testament corpus, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah, with the English rendering “Tamah” in one instance and “Tamah” represented by the same name in the other. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and list context.

word:hebrew:H8600.explanation: Tefotsah means a dispersal or dispersion.

word:hebrew:H886.explanation: Bᵉʼêrôthîy means a Beerothite, a person from Beeroth.

word:hebrew:H95.explanation: Agorah means a small silver coin, expressed in the passage as a piece of silver.

word:hebrew:H954.explanation: Buwsh means to be ashamed. It can also describe being confounded or disappointed.

word:hebrew:H998.explanation: Bîynâh means understanding. Scripture places it alongside wisdom in the context of keeping Yahweh’s instruction.
